paper_title: WorldMemBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Memory of Video World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As video models enable longer and more realistic interactive experiences, maintaining a world consistent with its history becomes essential. This requires both preserving previously observed content and ensuring coherent world evolution over time. World memory is a critical capability to evaluate alongside visual fidelity and video duration. We introduce WorldMemBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating world memory in video world models. Across 260 test cases, it assesses static memory through the retention of human identity and appearance, object appearance and geometry, and environmental content and geometry, and dynamic memory through event progression and state persistence. Using controlled camera departures and multi-revisit trajectories, the benchmark evaluates static content against fixed initial references and dynamic events against expected state transitions. It combines appearance and geometry metrics with event-specific assessments, and reports video quality and camera-following accuracy as complementary diagnostics. Evaluation of nine representative models shows that strong static retention does not imply reliable dynamic state evolution, while repeated revisits reveal memory degradation beyond the first return. Human studies support the alignment between our automatic evaluations and human judgments. WorldMemBench provides a systematic testbed for diagnosing memory failures and guiding the development of persistent, temporally coherent video worlds.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recent advances in autoregressive video generation have enabled longer, more coherent video sequences Huang et al. (2025b); Zhu et al. (2026b); Zhao et al. (2026). In parallel, camera-controlled methods have improved viewpoint and trajectory control Bai et al. (2025). Together, these developments support video world models that enable sustained, interactive exploration of generated environments Mao et al. (2025); Gao et al. (2026); Yin et al. (2026); Sun et al. (2025). Such exploration repeatedly moves content into and out of view, requiring generated worlds to remain consistent with past observations and events. We define world memory as the ability to preserve established content and sustain coherent state evolution across interruptions in observation. Static content, including human identities, object appearance and geometry, and scene layouts, should remain consistent across revisits. Meanwhile, ongoing events should progress coherently while out of view, with their expected consequences reflected upon return. Visual quality and local temporal coherence alone cannot establish these capabilities. Recent benchmarks have begun to assess memory-related failures, including revisit consistency Zhang et al. (2026); Gu et al. (2026); Xu et al. (2026a) and state evolution under interrupted observation Chen et al. (2026); Ma et al. (2026); Lu et al. (2026); Duan et al. (2026). LoopBench Wu et al. (2026) further evaluates scene recall across multi-revisit trajectories. Building on these efforts, an important question is how memory behaves throughout continued exploration. successful return demonstrates recovery at one moment, but provides only partial evidence of reliability over subsequent interactions. Repeated revisits help determine whether recovered content remains stable, whether evolving states remain consistent with prior events, and how these behaviors respond to changes in exploration direction. Tab. 1 compares benchmark coverage and highlights our joint assessment of memory persistence over extended exploration and repeated revisits, off-screen state evolution, and physical consistency. To this end, we introduce WorldMemBench, benchmark for systematically evaluating memory in video world models. It comprises 260 cases across 23 semantic categories, including 200 staticmemory cases and 60 dynamic-memory cases as in Fig. 1. Our evaluation covers four dimensions. Static Memory assesses retention of human identity and appearance, object appearance and geometry, and environmental content and geometry. Dynamic Memory evaluates event progression, state persistence, and causal and physical plausibility. General Video Quality and Camera Following serve as complementary diagnostics of perceptual quality and adherence to prescribed exploration trajectories. Reporting these diagnostics separately helps interpret memory performance when rendering quality or camera accuracy differs across models. In WorldMemBench, we use controlled trajectories for leaving and revisiting observed content, including translation loops, repeated rotations about the same axis, and rotations that switch axes between revisits. Each static revisit is compared with the same initial reference to track deviations across successive returns. Dynamic cases specify an initial state, an action, and an expected next state. Case-specific checklists assess event onset and whether subsequent observations reflect its expected progression and consequences. Dynamic memory is thus evaluated through coherent state changes rather than similarity to an unchanged initial frame. Our evaluation of nine video world models reveals that strong static retention does not necessarily imply reliable dynamic evolution: HY-WorldPlay leads all seven static metrics but initiates only 31.7% of prescribed events. Repeated revisits expose cumulative degradation that persists on posequalified returns, while switching rotation axes adds further drop of 0.152 in Environment Visible. Human studies show agreement between our automatic metrics and human judgments. We use WorldMemBench to examine how context access affects memory, comparing training-free policies while holding the model and generation settings fixed. Combining recent context with view-relevant history improves most evaluated memory metrics and reduces latency relative to full-history access. These results demonstrate the value of WorldMemBench for characterizing memory limitations and evaluating context-access strategies. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce WorldMemBench, benchmark comprising 260 cases across 23 categories, with 200 static-memory cases covering humans, objects, and environments and 60 dynamic-memory cases covering seven types of off-screen state transitions.

sections.title: 3 WORLDMEMBENCH CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: In this section, we describe the construction of WorldMemBench, including its data composition and camera trajectory design. The benchmark evaluates world memory through controlled departureand-revisit rollouts, probing whether previously observed content and evolving states remain consistent across periods outside the cameras field of view. 3.1 EVALUATION DIMENSIONS Inspired by hierarchical diagnostic evaluation Yang et al. (2026), we organize evaluation into four complementary dimensions. Static Memory assesses the retention of previously observed humans, objects, and environments upon revisitation, covering individual entities through global scene structure. Dynamic Memory examines whether events progress appropriately while out of view and whether their consequences persist upon return. Each case specifies an initial state, an action, and next state, with assessment covering event progression, state persistence, final-state correctness, and causal and physical consistency. These two memory dimensions are complemented by General Video Quality, which measures imaging and aesthetic quality, and Camera Following, which evaluates adherence to the prescribed camera motion. Together, they characterize memory performance alongside the visual quality and control accuracy of the generated rollouts. 3.2 DATA COMPOSITION WorldMemBench comprises 260 core cases across four families: 60 Human, 70 Object, 70 Environment, and 60 Dynamic Memory cases. The first three families form the 200-case Static Memory subset. General Video Quality is evaluated on all static-memory rollouts, while Camera Following reuses 85 static-memory cases suitable for trajectory evaluation. As shown in Fig. 2, the four case families jointly cover 23 representative content categories. sections.title: 5.1 SETUP
sections.content: We evaluate nine models across all dimensions of WorldMemBench: HY-WorldPlay Sun et al. (2025), Matrix-Game 3 Wang et al. (2026), Matrix-Game 3.5 Qian et al. (2026), SANA-WM Zhu et al. (2026a), YUME Mao et al. (2025), LingBot-World Team et al. (2026b), LingBot-World-v2 Gao et al. (2026), Evoke Yin et al. (2026), and DreamX-World Team et al. (2026a). All models are evaluated under consistent benchmark conditions using unified evaluation protocol, with each model configured according to the defaults provided in its official release. Model-specific resolutions, frame rates, temporal generation strategies, control adaptations, and inference settings are detailed in Appendix C. 5.2 EVALUATION OF WORLD MODELS Quantitative Results. Following the evaluation protocol, we evaluate videos generated by nine world models across four dimensions: General Video Quality, Static Memory, Dynamic Memory, and Camera Following. Tab. 2 reveals distinct strengths across these dimensions. HY-WorldPlay leads all seven Static Memory metrics, demonstrating strong retention of human, object, and environmental content. However, its Dynamic Memory score is substantially lower than those of LingBot-World and YUME, which achieve the highest and second-highest scores, respectively. These results suggest that preserving static content and maintaining evolving states pose distinct challenges. Camera-following performance also varies: Matrix-Game 3 achieves the lowest translation error, while HY-WorldPlay achieves the lowest rotation error. Overall, no model leads across all four dimensions, highlighting the need to evaluate complementary capabilities separately. Qualitative Results. To examine whether our metrics reflect observable memory behavior, we present an Environment multi-revisit comparison in Fig. 4, with Human and Object comparisons in Appendix E. In the Human, Object, and Environment cases shown in Figs. 6, 7, and 4, HYWorldPlay most consistently preserves subject identity, object geometry, and scene layout across three revisits. These observations align with its first-place performance on all seven Static Memory metrics in Tab. 2, providing qualitative support for our quantitative evaluation of memory consistency across different content types and repeated revisits. Human Evaluation. To complement the qualitative analysis, we assess how well our Static and Dynamic Memory metrics align with human judgments. For Static Memory (Tab. 6), blinded A/B agreement ranges from 78.5% to 92.5% across the six metrics, with model-level Spearman correlations ranging from 0.301 (Environment Depth) to 0.988 (Environment Visible). For Dynamic Memory (Tab. 7), the checklist judge achieves Spearman correlation of 0.732 and Pearson linear correlation coefficient (PLCC) of 0.808 for the Overall score across 50 instances. Complete annotation protocols, per-dimension results, and interfaces are provided in Appendix F. Together, these results support the validity of our metrics for assessing world memory. 5.3 MULTI-REVISIT ANALYSIS Fig. 5 shows how the seven Static Memory metrics and Camera Rotation RPE change across nine models from R1 to R3 under LRLRLR, revealing two main findings: 1) Multi-Revisit Evaluation Exposes Cumulative Memory Decay. Nine-model averages degrade monotonically across revisits on all eight metrics: Object Appearance, Human Identity, and Object Geometry drop by 0.229, 0.217, and 0.205 from R1 to R3, while Environment Reconstruction Score decreases by 0.196. The trend also holds per model: on the Human, Object, Environment Visible, and Environment Reconstruction metrics, every model is weaker at R3 than at R1, and Environment Depth degrades for eight of the nine models. Content recovered on the first return therefore does not necessarily persist across later revisits; multi-revisit evaluation exposes cumulative memory decay that single-return evalua-

Budgeted retrieval of view-relevant history has been proposed to extend the memory of video world models Yu et al. (2025); Yi et al. (2026); we use WorldMemBench to examine which memory dimensions such policies help. To examine how context access affects these capabilities, we compare three training-free policies on LingBot World v2, keeping the model and other generation settings fixed. FullKV provides access to the complete history. Sliding Windows uses recent context within fixed budget, while FoV combines recent context with view-relevant historical chunks under the same budget. FoV achieves the best scores on eight of the eleven capability metrics and outperforms Sliding Windows on all eleven. Compared with FullKV, it scores higher on all four Dynamic Memory sub-metrics and both Human metrics. FullKV, however, retains an advantage in Object Appearance, Object Geometry, and Environment Visible, suggesting that the benefits of context selection vary across memory dimensions. Both budgeted policies also reduce inference time. Across 660 matched videos, mean end-to-end latency is 322.2 for FullKV, compared with 262.7 for FoV and 260.4 for Sliding Windows. These correspond to speedups of 1.23 and 1.24, respectively. Overall, the results suggest that combining recent context with view-relevant history offers favorable balance between memory performance and efficiency. Context budgets, evaluation sets, timing protocols, and further analysis are provided in Appendix H.

Multi-revisit evaluation reveals cumulative memory degradation beyond the first return, while cross-axis revisits expose additional sensitivity to changes in exploration direction. Human studies further support the alignment between automatic assessments and human judgments. With the model and generation settings held fixed, controlled context-access study reveals how different temporal context policies affect memory performance and inference efficiency. Together, these findings establish WorldMemBench as both an evaluation benchmark and diagnostic tool for improving world memory. We hope that this benchmark will help advance video world models toward reliable simulators that support long-term interaction, learning, and planning in persistent virtual environments.

sections.title: C INFERENCE SETTINGS
sections.content: All formal inference runs on machines equipped with eight NVIDIA H20-3e GPUs. Every model uses frozen random seeds and inference configurations, so that no setting varies across cases or trajectories. HY-WorldPlay. HY-WorldPlay consumes per-frame OpenCV camera-to-world poses; we extract one latent camera anchor every four pixel frames and generate its native pose condition with fixed camera intrinsics. Formal inference uses seed 1, 4-step distilled AR sampling, and eight-card model parallelism, with prompt rewriting and super-resolution disabled. Matrix-Game 3. The native interface of Matrix-Game 3 is jointly controlled by keyboard translation and mouse rotation. We compile the normalized camera trajectory into per-frame keyboard/mouse conditions. The model runs 12 iterations with seed 42 and 3-step AR sampling: the first segment generates 57 frames and each subsequent iteration adds 40 frames, producing 497 frames in total; inference uses seven GPUs for diffusion and one GPU for asynchronous MG-LightVAE decoding. Matrix-Game 3.5. Matrix-Game 3.5 constructs its native PRoPE condition from per-case camera intrinsics and camera-to-world poses. Formal inference adopts the released six-block distilled configuration, where each block corresponds to 84 camera poses, with three-step schedule of [1000, 667, 333] and seed 3407. The six blocks share the same content prompt and complete continuous 505-frame rollout through the generated history and dynamic context. SANA-WM. SANA-WM builds chunk-level Plucker conditions from per-case camera intrinsics and poses, and generates videos through streaming pipeline consisting of stage-1, refiner, and causal VAE. Stage-1 uses 4-step self-forcing sampling, and both stage-1 and the refiner treat three latent frames as one temporal block; formal inference fixes seed 42 and outputs 481 frames. YUME. YUME does not directly consume numerical camera poses. We convert the normalized trajectory into segmented camera captions composed of Left, Right, Up, Down, Hold, and translation directions; each caption stage corresponds to 29 frames, and the MemoryBench content prompt is appended verbatim to every stage. Formal inference disables additional prompt refinement and uses seed 43 with 4-step Euler sampling; LRLR and LRUD produce 493 frames, while LRLRLR, which contains three revisits, produces 551 frames. LingBot World. LingBot World interpolates per-frame camera-to-world poses to the latent rate and converts them into framewise relative poses and Plucker conditions; camera intrinsics are fixed on the models input canvas. We set the chunk size to four latent frames so that the 493-frame target trajectory is generated in full, and run eight-card causal AR inference with seed 1 and FullKV attention. LingBot World v2. sections.title: D DYNAMIC MEMORY EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: D.1 ASSESSMENT PROTOCOL Each rollout is sampled at fixed stride of 8 frames, always including the first and last frames. The sampled frames are provided to Qwen3.8-27B in chronological order, together with the checklist and the planned camera-phase ranges (initial hold, departures, revisits, and final stationary hold). These ranges allow the assessment model to locate the evidence window for each question without access to the generation prompt. The model first determines whether the central event visibly starts during the initial hold and then answers all eight questions. If the model determines that the event has not visibly started, all eight question scores are set to zero. Otherwise, each question receives one point if the models answer matches the frozen reference answer. We set max tokens to 4096 for the assessment model. D.2 EVENT INITIATION AND CONDITIONAL DYNAMIC SCORES We separate the event-start prerequisite from subsequent checklist performance using the same 60 videos per model. The event-start rate pstart is the fraction of videos judged to show concrete event progress during the initial hold. The conditional score Scond averages the eight-question checklist score only over those videos. Because videos with negative gate receive zero, the reported Overall satisfies Sgated = pstartScond. HY-WorldPlay has conditional score of 0.928 on 19 started events, but its 31.7% start rate yields gated Overall of 0.294. LingBot World starts 56 of 60 events and obtains conditional score of 0.866, yielding 0.808 overall. Thus, differences in the headline Dynamic Memory scores reflect both event initiation and subsequent checklist performance. Matrix-Game 3s conditional score of 0.917 is based on only three videos. We retain the gated score as the end-to-end benchmark result and use the decomposition to distinguish these sources of failure. The conditional scores remain judge-based evaluations of different successful-start subsets, not isolated measures of memory.

sections.content: Static Memory protocol. We conduct blinded A/B preference study on whether the six Static Memory metrics reproduce human judgments of long-term memory retention. In total, 504 blinded pairs are each judged by three annotators as A-wins, Tie, or B-wins, with model identities and order hidden, yielding 1,512 judgements (252 per metric). Pairwise agreement between the automatic metric and the human majority-vote direction serves as the primary measure; we further compare model-level win rates (Win/Tie/Loss as 1/0.5/0) via Spearman ρ. Pairwise agreement compares the automatic preference with decisive human majority. Majority ties and three-way A/Tie/B splits are excluded from this denominator and reported separately. For example, Human Identity has 65 agreements among 76 decisive pairs, giving 85.5%; one majority tie and seven three-way splits account for the remaining eight pairs. ANALYSIS OF CONTEXT-ACCESS POLICIES In this section, we examine the capability differences induced by temporal KV-access policies in Section 5.5, detailing the controlled setup and the accompanying capability analysis. Controlled Experimental Setup. We compare FullKV, Sliding Windows, and FoV on LingBot World v2 without retraining. We fix the checkpoint, conditioning first frame, text prompt, camera trajectory, random seed, number of sampling steps, generation length, and evaluators. The temporal KV-access policy during autoregressive generation is the only variable. FullKV allows the current chunk to access the entire historical KV context. Sliding Windows uses fixed budget of 20 latents: 4 sink, 12 recent, and 4 current latents. FoV uses the same 20-latent budget, comprising 4 sink, 4 recent, 8 retrieved, and 4 current latents. The retrieved latents come from two historical chunks selected by current-to-history field-of-view overlap. The fixed-budget comparison therefore tests how allocating context to view-relevant history affects memory beyond access to recent observations. Evaluation coverage and timing. All three policies use identical evaluation sets: 180 Human, 210 Object, 210 Environment, and 60 Dynamic Memory videos, totaling 660 matched videos per policy. Latency is the mean end-to-end time to generate 493-frame video over this matched set. Speedup is the ratio of FullKVs mean latency to the corresponding policys mean latency. View-relevant context for static retention. Across 490 Environment revisit slots, FoV increases the proportion of returns that reach the target viewpoint from 57.6% to 65.3% and reduces the mean return rotation error from 31.0 to 26.7 relative to FullKV. These gains accompany improvements in Human Identity, Human Appearance, Environment Depth, and Environment Reconstruction, suggesting that view-relevant historical context supports both scene recovery and content retention. The deadlift example in Fig. 10 illustrates the difference in viewpoint recovery: FoV returns to more complete view of the lifter and barbell, whereas FullKV retains close-up dominated by the weight plates. Context allocation for dynamic progression. Maintaining dynamic memory requires the model to preserve the latest event state while allowing it to evolve. Sliding Windows matches FullKV on Return Progress (0.667), improves Final State from 0.592 to 0.600, but scores lower on Persistence/Reset (0.717 vs. 0.733) and Causal/Physics (0.775 vs. 0.792). Prioritizing recent observations alone therefore does not consistently improve dynamic memory. FoV combines recent context with view-relevant historical evidence and achieves further gains over both baselines across all four submetrics. The erasing example in Fig. 10 also reveals differences in the consistency of task-relevant objects: Sliding Windows produces visibly enlarged erasing object, while FoV maintains compact eraser in contact with the paper during the returned sequence. Together, the quantitative comparison and these examples favor combining recent states with view-relevant historical context over recent-only window.

sections.title: I LIMITATION AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: The current benchmark focuses on controlled translation and rotation trajectories over rollouts of several hundred frames. Longer horizons, free-form or compound traversal patterns, and embodied settings in which camera and object actions are jointly selected remain outside its present scope. Dynamic Memory additionally relies on frozen case-specific checklists evaluated by VLM. Although the resulting scores show strong overall agreement with human judgments, the Causal/Physics dimension remains the most challenging sub-dimension. Extending the benchmark to richer event types, multi-agent interactions, and longer unobserved phases, together with stronger and more diverse evaluators, would further test the limits of persistent world generation. We hope WorldMemBench serves as practical testbed for developing video world models that remember, evolve, and remain consistent over extended interaction.
